01 / Context

Automation was fast. Trust was missing.

This concept explores a workflow where an LLM groups search terms and suggests negative keywords. The design challenge is giving specialists enough context to evaluate a recommendation before any account change.

Product problem: Turn opaque suggestions into decisions that a paid-search specialist can confidently inspect, edit, approve, or reject.
02 / Constraints

Bad negatives have asymmetric cost.

AAn overly broad negative could suppress a converting search theme.
BSpecialists needed the underlying terms, spend, and conversion context.
CEvery action needed an understandable reason and audit trail.
DThe review flow still had to be quicker than inspecting thousands of terms manually.
03 / Decision

Evidence before action.

Rather than a flat list with one-click application, the proposed experience uses theme-level cards with supporting data, editable match types, confidence explanations, and an explicit decision per recommendation.

Not selectedOpaque suggestion listAn “Apply all” button. Easy to click; hard to verify.
Selected directionEvidence-first cardsTerms and costs visible, editable suggestion, reject-with-reason, and reviewable export.
04 / Prototype

Review suggestions yourself.

Approve, edit, or reject proposals, try an exception state, and inspect the local decision log.

Decision history
No actions yet.

Sample terms only. Nothing is connected to Google Ads.

05 / Outcome

Optimize for adoption and decision quality.

The experience is designed to measure time per review, edit rate, rejection reasons, and unintended exclusions. This prototype has not been evaluated in a measured live-account pilot.

Because suggestions are staged for review rather than directly applied, the operator remains accountable for account changes.

06 / Reflection

Next: better confidence calibration.

Confidence should account for recency as well as conversions. Structured rejection reasons would make recurring model failures easier to analyze. A larger validation set across both automotive and insurance accounts would test whether the taxonomy generalizes.
